intro: Marketing ROI nets marketing cost out of the revenue it produced, so it answers whether the spend actually paid for itself. Enter attributed revenue and marketing cost to get the percentage.

sections.heading: How Marketing ROI is calculated
sections.body: Marketing ROI = (Revenue − Cost) ÷ Cost, shown as a percentage — [the same revenue-minus-cost-over-cost shape Salesforce uses to define marketing ROI](https://www.salesforce.com/marketing/analytics/roi-guide/). Cost subtracts out of the numerator first, which is what separates this from a plain revenue-to-spend ratio: the result already nets out what was spent before expressing the return.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: ($5,000 − $1,000) ÷ $1,000 = 400.00%. The net return above the entered marketing cost was $4,000 — four times the $1,000 cost, on top of getting that $1,000 back. That's a different statement than saying revenue was four times spend; ROI already has the cost subtracted out before the ratio is taken.

sections.heading: Marketing ROI vs. ROAS
sections.body: These two numbers come from the same shape of calculation, but they're not automatically the same quantity. When both metrics use the exact same attributed revenue and the exact same cost denominator, ROI (as a decimal) equals [ROAS](/calculators/roas) minus 1, since ROAS is revenue ÷ cost and ROI is (revenue − cost) ÷ cost. In the worked example, 5,000 ÷ 1,000 gives a 5.00x ROAS, while (5,000 − 1,000) ÷ 1,000 gives a 400% ROI — the same underlying result here, read as a gross revenue multiple in one case and a net-of-cost percentage in the other. That identity only holds when the two costs match, though: ROAS commonly uses ad spend alone, while Marketing ROI is often computed from a broader marketing-cost figure that also folds in agency or creative fees. If the cost definitions differ, the two numbers stop describing the same spend and the algebraic relationship breaks.

sections.heading: What Marketing ROI tells you, and what it doesn't
sections.body: Marketing ROI tells you whether attributed revenue covered the marketing cost and by how much — a straightforward answer to 'did this spend pay for itself.' It doesn't tell you whether the business as a whole was profitable. The cost in this formula is marketing cost specifically; it has no visibility into cost of goods sold, fulfillment, or any other expense behind what was sold. A 400% marketing ROI on a product with thin margins can still leave less real profit than a lower ROI on a high-margin one, because this ratio never sees that cost at all — only the marketing spend it was actually computed against.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
items: Reading Marketing ROI and ROAS as roughly the same size. A 400% ROI and a 5x ROAS from the same numbers look like very different magnitudes at a glance, even though they describe the identical result.

Treating Marketing ROI as overall business profitability. It only nets out marketing cost — product cost, fulfillment, and other expenses aren't in the formula, so a strong ROI doesn't confirm the business made money on what was sold.

Changing what counts as "cost" between calculations. Comparing an ROI computed from media spend alone against one that also folds in agency and creative fees moves the number for reasons that have nothing to do with performance.
Attributing revenue from a broader window or channel mix than the cost actually covers. Revenue and cost need to describe the same marketing activity, or the ratio doesn't measure what it appears to.

faq.a: Marketing ROI is the net return a marketing campaign generated relative to what it cost, calculated as (revenue − cost) ÷ cost and expressed as a percentage. It's an efficiency metric, not a profitability metric: unlike a plain revenue-to-spend ratio, ROI subtracts the cost out of the numerator first, so the result already reflects the net return above cost rather than the gross return. A 400% ROI means the campaign generated a net return four times its entered marketing cost, on top of recovering the original spend. Marketing ROI is specific to marketing cost, though — it has no visibility into product cost, fulfillment, or other business expenses, so it answers whether the marketing spend paid for itself, not whether the business as a whole was profitable on what was sold.

faq.q: How do you calculate Marketing ROI?
faq.a: Subtract cost from revenue, then divide by cost: Marketing ROI = (Revenue − Cost) ÷ Cost. A campaign that generated $5,000 in attributed revenue from $1,000 in marketing cost has an ROI of ($5,000 − $1,000) ÷ $1,000 = 400.00%. Both numbers need to describe the same marketing activity and time period — revenue attributed to a broader channel mix than the cost actually covers produces a ratio that overstates performance. Cost should also stay consistently defined between calculations; comparing one ROI computed from media spend alone against another that also includes agency or creative fees moves the result for reasons unrelated to how the campaigns actually performed.

faq.q: Is Marketing ROI the same as ROAS?
faq.a: They're mathematically linked under matching definitions, but not automatically the same number. ROAS is revenue ÷ cost, a gross multiple; Marketing ROI is (revenue − cost) ÷ cost, a net-of-cost percentage. When both use the exact same revenue and the exact same cost denominator, ROI as a decimal equals ROAS minus 1 — a 5.00x ROAS and a 400% ROI from those matching numbers are the identical result read from different reference points. That relationship depends on the cost definitions lining up, though: ROAS commonly uses ad spend alone, while Marketing ROI can be computed from a broader marketing-cost figure. Use ROAS when comparing gross revenue efficiency across campaigns with a consistent cost definition; use ROI when the question is specifically whether the spend generated a net return above its own cost.

Yes. A negative Marketing ROI means the campaign generated less revenue than it cost — for example, $800 in attributed revenue from $1,000 in marketing cost gives (800 − 1,000) ÷ 1,000 = −20%. That's a real, valid result: it means the campaign lost money on marketing cost alone, before any other business expense is even considered. Unlike ROAS, which can never go below 0x since both revenue and spend are non-negative, ROI can go below −100% in principle if a campaign somehow produced negative attributed revenue, though in practice a −100% ROI (zero revenue against the full cost) is usually the practical floor. Any ROI below 0% means the marketing spend didn't recover its own cost.

faq.q: Does a high Marketing ROI mean the campaign was profitable for the business overall?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Marketing ROI only nets out the marketing cost entered into the calculation — it has no visibility into cost of goods sold, fulfillment, payment processing, or any other expense behind what was actually sold. A campaign can post a strong 400% marketing ROI and still contribute less real profit than a lower-ROI campaign, if the product being sold carries thin margins once those other costs are counted. Marketing ROI answers a narrower question: did the marketing spend itself generate a net gain. Whether the business made money overall depends on margin and every other cost this ratio was never built to see, which is a separate calculation from the marketing-cost-only number this page computes.
